forces: Mixed chorus and orchestra; instrumental personnel uncredited
performers: Oratorio Chorus; conductor and accompanying players uncredited
intro: The Oratorio Chorus brings Handel’s Hallelujah to an Edison Diamond Disc in 1916. Four choral parts turn a handful of biblical phrases into shouts, long proclamations and pursuing tunes.

sections.label: A · Hallelujah
sections.mNote: The choir’s short cries and answering instrumental phrases

sections.label: B · The choir sings together
sections.mNote: Longer phrases interrupt the quick acclamations

sections.label: C · Held notes and quick answers
sections.mNote: Long proclamations above the moving choral parts

sections.label: D · The voices gather again
sections.mNote: The choir combines its leaping tune and repeated cries

sections.label: Coda · The last Hallelujah
sections.mNote: The final statement closes in D major

cues.title: One word, four voices
cues.text: The choir begins with short, shared cries of “Hallelujah”. Soon Handel has the parts pursuing one another through longer lines. The same four voices can sound like a crowd speaking together or four people all eager to speak.
cues.evidence: Handel, Messiah, Hallelujah, opening choral declarations and subsequent imitative passages; Joshua Koo’s Mutopia full score. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Handel on an Edison disc
cues.text: In May 1916 Edison issues this performance on Diamond Disc 80292. The singers appear on the label as the Oratorio Chorus. Handel’s great public celebration now fits on one side of a record.
cues.evidence: Thomas Edison National Historical Park catalogue: recording 1916, release May 1916, Diamond Disc 80292-R, Oratorio Chorus. https://www.nps.gov/edis/learn/photosmultimedia/opera-vocal-and-choral.htm

cues.title: Jennens’s scripture collection
cues.text: In the summer of 1741 Charles Jennens sends Handel a collection of passages from the Old and New Testaments. It tells no continuous story. Part I is prophecy and birth, Part II death and resurrection, Part III the believer’s response.
cues.evidence: Teresa M. Neff, Handel and Haydn Society programme notes: Jennens’s assembled text, sent in summer 1741, and its three parts. https://handelandhaydn.org/interactive-program-notes-handels-messiah/

cues.title: Room for more in Dublin
cues.text: For the first Messiah, in Dublin in April 1742, demand is so great that the organisers ask men to leave their swords at home and women to come without hooped skirts. They need every inch of the Music Hall in Fishamble Street.
cues.evidence: Teresa M. Neff quotes the Dublin Journal’s announcement and gives the première as 13 April 1742, Music Hall, Fishamble Street. https://handelandhaydn.org/interactive-program-notes-handels-messiah/

cues.title: Two lengths of note
cues.text: Handel gives “King of kings” long notes and “Hallelujah” quick ones. The choir can proclaim both at once: one part holds its place while another dances around it.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 51–68 and 74–89: sustained proclamations combined with shorter choral replies. This describes the later chorus as a whole. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The final broad Hallelujah
cues.text: At the close Handel brings the choir together for one last, spacious “Hallelujah”. The bass moves from G to D, and the final D major chord carries a fermata: everyone holds the same ending.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, closing bars 92–94; the cue uses the recording’s established closing section. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Densmore’s catalogue transcription describes Edison 80292-R as ‘Mixed voices with orchestra — Oratorio Chorus’. The orchestra’s identity, conductor and individual players are not credited; Edison is the record company, not a performer.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The catalogue describes mixed voices with orchestra, but no performing edition, arranger or individual instruments are established. No specific orchestral substitution or match to Handel’s original scoring is inferred from that generic credit.

composer.epithet: He filled London theatres with Italian opera, then put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg offered something noisier: a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant; Prince Ruspoli gave him singers and instrumentalists to write for. The Dixit Dominus of 1707 sends five choral parts racing through a Latin psalm, then makes them hold dissonant notes while the other voices move underneath. His chamber cantatas tried the same arts of persuasion with a single singer. Corelli’s Rome taught him what a violin could say beside a voice.
